title: The Waitress Who Repeated the Order
text:
In 2003 Rick van Baaren and his colleagues at the University of Nijmegen in the Netherlands took research on mimicry out of the lab and into a Dutch restaurant. They wanted to know whether being imitated makes people more generous.

A waitress was instructed to handle orders in one of two ways, decided in advance for each table. In one condition, she repeated the customer's order back to them word for word, exactly as they had said it. In the other, she confirmed the order with brief positive phrases such as "okay" or "coming up," without repeating the words. Everything else about her service was meant to be the same. At the end of the meal, the researchers recorded the tips.

Customers whose orders had been repeated verbatim left noticeably larger tips on average, and more of them left a tip at all. A second study, which compared mimicry with ordinary service, confirmed that repeating the order was what made the difference. Hearing their own words echoed back seemed to make customers feel understood.
lesson: Repeating back what someone said shows that you heard them, and people reward that. In a conversation, try reflecting their own words before adding yours.
people: Rick van Baaren, Rob Holland, B. Steenaert, Ad van Knippenberg
source: van Baaren, R. B., Holland, R. W., Steenaert, B., and van Knippenberg, A. (2003). Mimicry for money: Behavioral consequences of imitation. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 39(4), 393-398.
